items.text: With one-line descriptions, Claude cannot tell that the three channels are alternatives rather than complements. Tool descriptions should say when to use each tool relative to the others, so stating each channel's use case and that exactly one channel is chosen per notification (C) fixes the cause. A system-prompt rule (A) is a weaker, global patch that leaves the tools themselves ambiguous. A PostToolUse hook (B) runs after a call has already executed, so it cannot cancel later calls; blocking a call is a PreToolUse job. Renaming the tools (D) groups them visually but still gives Claude no rule for choosing between them.
items.why: Erklaerung an neuen Distraktor anpassen, B korrekt begruenden, Verweis auf nicht vorhandene 'check preferences'-Option entfernen.

items.match: Restrict the agent's OS-level file permissions
items.text: Add `/var/app/data/` to `additionalDirectories` so Claude Code confines every Write or Edit call to it.
items.why: OS-Dateirechte erzwingen die Grenze ebenfalls (Stamm spricht sogar von 'infrastructure level'); neuer Distraktor: additionalDirectories erweitert den Zugriff, beschraenkt ihn nicht.

items.text: A pre-tool-call (PreToolUse) hook validates the target path before the Write or Edit runs and denies the call, so the modification never happens, and it works without touching the system prompt. A post-tool-call hook (C) fires only after the file was already changed. A system-prompt instruction (D) is probabilistic and can be overridden. `additionalDirectories` (B) grants Claude access to extra directories; it widens what can be reached and does not confine writes to the listed path.
items.why: Erklaerung an neuen Distraktor B anpassen.

items.replace: A third-party MCP tool, whose server you cannot modify, returns a 50-field JSON object
items.why: Ein fields-Parameter (D) waere bei eigenem Server ebenfalls vertretbar; Stamm schliesst Aenderungen am Server aus.

items.text: A PostToolUse hook can replace the result Claude sees via `updatedToolOutput`, for MCP and built-in tools alike, so trimming each lookup to the 6 relevant fields stops the bloat before it accumulates over a multi-turn session. Adding a `fields` parameter (D) would be good tool design, but the server is third-party and cannot be changed. A system-prompt instruction to ignore fields (C) saves no tokens, because the fields are still in context. A larger context window (B) only postpones the problem and raises cost.
items.why: Erklaerung an eingegrenzten Stamm anpassen und updatedToolOutput (alle Tools) nennen.

items.text: `allowedTools` only auto-approves the tools it lists; it does not restrict Claude to them. Calls that need no approval run whether or not they are listed, and the Agent tool (formerly Task, which still works as an alias) is one of them, so leaving it out changes nothing (D). The thin single-agent response therefore has another cause, for example subagent descriptions too vague for Claude to delegate; clearer descriptions or naming the subagent in the prompt fix that. To actually stop spawning, put `Agent` in `disallowedTools`. A, B and C describe behaviors that don't exist.

items.text: A subagent's tool access is set by the `tools` field of its AgentDefinition: listing `["WebSearch"]` gives the subagent only that tool, while omitting the field inherits every tool available to subagents. `allowedTools` on the query only auto-approves the listed tools; it does not restrict which tools exist, so it cannot enforce least privilege. `tool_scope` and `tool_filter` are not AgentDefinition fields.
items.why: Erklaerung samt alter Correction-Notiz neu, passend zum neuen Schluessel.

items.text: A key that expired, was rotated, or has been revoked
items.why: Fehlende Berechtigungen liefern 403 permission_error, nicht 401 authentication_error.

items.text: Authentication failures point at the credential rather than the payload: a 401 authentication_error means the API key itself is invalid, expired, or revoked, while a key that merely lacks permission returns a 403 permission_error instead. A transient fault (A) presents differently, and neither prompt length (B) nor deprecation (D) produces an auth error.
items.why: 401 vs. 403 laut Fehler-Doku getrennt.

items.text: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop treats model output as untrusted input and lets the model self-correct. With strict tool use (`strict: true`) or Structured Outputs, constrained decoding guarantees schema-compliant output, so the retry loop becomes the fallback for paths without that guarantee and for semantic checks. Returning an empty object (A) hides the failure, firmer wording (B) still leaves compliance to chance, and regex patching (C) invents data.
items.why: Erklärung nennt jetzt strict/Structured Outputs als heutige Garantie statt eines erzwungenen tool_choice.

items.match: Declare the shape as a tool schema
items.text: Declare the shape as a JSON schema the output must match
items.why: Tool-Schema setzte ein erzwungenes tool_choice voraus (400 bei Opus/Sonnet 5.5); heute Structured Outputs.

items.text: A declared schema turns structure into a contract the response must satisfy, which is what a typed insert needs. Structured Outputs (`output_config.format` with a JSON schema) or a strict tool definition enforce it through constrained decoding. Asking in prose (A) and retrying on failure (B) both leave the shape to chance, and regular expressions over prose (C) are brittle by construction.
items.why: Erklärung auf Structured Outputs umgestellt.

items.text: It pushes tool execution into your network, where the tools can reach the database.
items.why: Mit self-hosted sandboxes läuft der Loop bei Anthropic, nur die Tools im eigenen Netz.

items.text: The tools have to execute somewhere that can reach the database, so network topology constrains the deployment. That means self-hosting, or with Managed Agents a self-hosted sandbox (Anthropic keeps running the loop, your worker executes the tool calls) or an MCP tunnel to a private MCP server in front of the database. Hosting choice is very much constrained by topology (A). Managed hosting doesn't grant arbitrary private-network reach (C), and network placement has nothing to do with whether the control flow is agentic (D).
items.why: Falsche Aussage „tool execution happens where the loop runs“ ersetzt.

items.find: not for being inherently safe.
items.replace: not for being inherently safe. In headless mode (`-p`) a call that needs approval is denied rather than waited on, so the tools CI may use must be allowed upfront (for example with `--allowedTools`, a hook, or `--permission-prompt-tool`).
items.why: -p lehnt freigabepflichtige Aufrufe ab, statt zu warten.

items.text: Auto mode replaces the human prompt with a classifier that blocks actions it judges risky; it reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety. So whatever must reliably bound the damage has to live in permissions and hooks, and deny rules still apply in every mode. Treating it as a drop-in (A) silently weakens a control. Auto mode doesn't ignore CLAUDE.md (C), since the classifier reads it, and model tier (D) is unrelated to the guardrail question.
items.why: Auto-Mode laut Doku: Klassifikator, keine Sicherheitsgarantie, Deny-Regeln greifen.

items.text: CLAUDE.md content, like a rule in .claude/rules/ without `paths` frontmatter, is loaded into every session; Skills stay dormant until their task arises. A biweekly procedure belongs in a Skill so it's supplied when relevant, not carried on every unrelated request. The file format (A) allows any prose, there's no convention forcing commands (C), and an always-loaded file is not the intended home for an occasional procedure (D).
items.why: „Rules are passive and permanent“ gilt nicht für Rules mit paths; präzisiert.

items.text: The MCP client is the intermediary: it discovers what the server offers, forwards calls, and returns results, which is why the server needs no knowledge of any conversation and stays independently deployable. With the Messages API's MCP connector, Anthropic's API plays that client role for remote servers you name, but it doesn't host every MCP server centrally (C). The model only emits tool calls (A) and has no network access of its own, and MCP servers don't relay calls to each other (D).
items.why: „The client is always the intermediary“ übersah den MCP connector.

items.text: Stable, reused context belongs in a Project's persistent instructions/knowledge sources — that's precisely the feature built for recurring work with shared background. Re-pasting each month (A) repeats work, research mode (C) looks online rather than at your guide, and one ever-growing thread (D) piles up context and degrades over time.

items.text: Uploaded documents don't update themselves, Drive-synced files (available only in private Projects) are only as current as their source, and instructions never change on their own. Without periodic review, a Project will keep confidently referencing outdated material as if it were still accurate — with no error and no warning to signal it.
items.why: „connected sources don't automatically stay current“ widersprach der Drive-Synchronisierung.

items.text: Structural guardrails enforced in code don't depend on the model reliably complying under every input; instruction-only guardrails (A, C) can still be violated on edge cases or adversarial input. Where the request uses Structured Outputs or strict tool use, constrained decoding already guarantees the schema, and code-level validation stays as the backstop and for semantic checks. Temperature (D) is no guardrail, and sampling parameters are removed as of API version 2026-10-21.
items.why: Structured Outputs als heutige Garantie ergänzt; temperature-Distraktor eingeordnet.
